prompt:
Compute absolute Spearman rank correlations between columns 2 to 8 and columns 9 to 17 and run a two-sided, p < 0.05 significance test on the correlations without correcting for multiple comparisons. Exclude subjects that appear to induce spurious correlations. Plot significant correlations in a matrix using the `plot_correlation_matrix` tool.

DATASET: correlates_common_subjects
  386 subjects. Symptoms + task measures only. Subject-level.
  386 rows, 386 subjects (1.0 rows per subject, subject-level)
  columns 2-8  (symptoms): 7-up, 7-down, GAD-7, BIS, BAS, SHAPS, PSWQ
  columns 9-17 (measures): Acc, Pts, WS, LS, Pers, beta, eta_p, eta_n, kappa
  63 correlations, uncorrected at alpha=0.05 -> ~3.2 false positives expected from noise alone

SUPPORTING TABLES (evidence for deciding who to exclude; they are NOT part of the correlation):
  task_data: 36,540 trial rows (~90/subject): block, trial, choice, rt, accuracy, outcome.
    36,540 rows, 9 columns, 406 subjects; columns: subject, block, trial, correct, choice, key, rt, accuracy, outcome

WHAT THE COLUMNS MEAN:
  7-up           7 Up mania/hypomania screen (higher = more symptoms)
  7-down         7 Down depression screen (higher = more symptoms)
  GAD-7          Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale
  BIS            Behavioural Inhibition System sensitivity
  BAS            Behavioural Activation System sensitivity
  SHAPS          Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (anhedonia)
  PSWQ           Penn State Worry Questionnaire
  Acc            proportion of correct choices in the reversal-learning task
  Pts            total points earned
  WS             win-stay rate: P(repeat choice | previous trial rewarded)
  LS             lose-shift rate: P(switch choice | previous trial unrewarded)
  Pers           perseveration: repeated choices after contingency reversal
  beta           inverse temperature from the RL model (choice determinism)
  eta_p          learning rate for positive prediction errors
  eta_n          learning rate for negative prediction errors
  kappa          choice-stickiness parameter

trace.thought: Initial correlation sweep to identify symptom-behaviour associations before exclusion of careless subjects.
Re-run correlation sweep excluding subjects flagged as careless to remove spurious correlations.
Plot significant correlations after excluding careless subjects to visualize symptom-behaviour relationships.

outcome.final_claim: After excluding 171 subjects flagged as careless based on task behavior proxies, 25 significant absolute Spearman rank correlations remain between symptom scales (7-up, 7-down, GAD-7, BIS, BAS, SHAPS, PSWQ) and task measures (Acc, Pts, WS, LS, Pers, beta, eta_p, eta_n, kappa) at p < 0.05 without multiple comparison correction. The strongest correlations involve the 7-up mania/hypomania scale negatively correlating with inverse temperature (beta, rho = -0.3794), win-stay rate (WS, rho = -0.3268), accuracy (Acc, rho = -0.295), and positively with lose-shift rate (LS, rho = 0.2847). Other symptoms such as BIS, 7-down, GAD-7, and PSWQ show weaker but still significant correlations with various task measures. The correlation matrix plot visually summarizes these significant relationships. The number and identity of significant correlations did not change after excluding flagged subjects, indicating these associations are not driven by spurious data from careless responders.
limitations: The correlations are uncorrected for multiple comparisons, so approximately 3.2 false positives are expected by chance among the 25 significant correlations.
The causal direction or underlying mechanisms of these associations cannot be determined from correlation alone.
The stability of these findings across other quality selection criteria or in independent replication samples was not assessed here.
Quality labels for ambiguous subjects (neither clearly attentive nor flagged careless) were not available, limiting refinement of inclusion decisions.
outcome.resolving_measurement: Applying multiple comparison correction methods, obtaining quality labels for ambiguous subjects, and replication in independent samples with similar symptom and task measures would settle the open questions about robustness and interpretation.
